content: 1. Danger Signs in Children: For children under 2 months, danger signs include poor feeding, movement only when stimulated or no movement at all, fast breathing (over 60 breaths per minute), severe chest in-drawing, fever (temperature above 38°C), or convulsions. For children aged 2 months to 3 years, danger signs include inability to drink or breastfeed, lethargy or unconsciousness, vomiting everything, convulsions, or fever above 38°C. 2. Nutritional Assessment: A child’s diet should include food from at least four of the following groups: grains, roots, tubers; legumes and nuts; dairy products; flesh foods (meat, fish, poultry, organ meats); eggs; vitamin A-rich fruits and vegetables; and other fruits and vegetables. Breastfed children aged 6–8 months should receive solid, semi-solid, or soft foods at least twice daily, while those aged 9–23 months should receive such foods three times daily. Non-breastfed children aged 6–23 months should receive solid, semi-solid, or soft foods or milk feeds at least four times daily. 3. Vaccination and Vitamin A: Vitamin A supplementation and deworming medication are recommended for children over 6 months and 12 months, respectively, in areas with high soil-transmitted infection prevalence. 4. Diarrhea Management: Health workers should assess the duration of diarrhea, presence of blood in stools, and signs of dehydration (e.g., sunken eyes, slow skin pinch). Management includes oral rehydration salts (ORS), zinc supplementation, continued feeding, and counseling on extra fluids. Antibiotics should only be prescribed for bloody diarrhea. 5. Cough and Breathing Difficulties: Health workers should evaluate the duration of cough, presence of wheezing, fast breathing, chest in-drawing, or stridor. A trial of inhaled medication may be given for wheezing. Persistent symptoms (over 14 days) may require referral for tuberculosis or asthma assessment. 6. Fever Management: Health workers should determine the duration of fever and assess for associated symptoms like stiff neck, rash, or bacterial infections. Malaria or dengue testing should be performed if suspected, and appropriate antimalarial or antipyretic treatment should be provided. 7. HIV Screening and Management: Caregivers and children should be tested for HIV. HIV-positive children should receive antiretroviral therapy (ART), co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, and counseling on feeding, home care, and follow-up. 8. Injury Prevention and Management: Caregivers should be aware of strategies to prevent injuries, such as supervising children near water, fire, or sharp objects, and ensuring safe play areas. Health workers should counsel on preventing future injuries and managing existing ones. 9. Early Childhood Development: Caregivers should engage in age-appropriate activities to promote development, such as interactive play, reading, and encouraging movement and communication. Developmental concerns, such as delayed speech or motor skills, should prompt further assessment and intervention. 10. Growth Monitoring: 11. Household Environment: Health workers should provide advice on improving water safety, hygiene, and ventilation. 12.
